lessons.title: Wood destroying organisms in South Africa
lessons.html:
Why timber pests matter

Timber is used in roof trusses, floors, doors, window frames, furniture, fencing, farm structures and packaging. Wood destroying organisms (WDOs) can weaken it until structures fail, causing costly repairs and safety hazards. In parts of South Africa, buyers and banks commonly require a timber pest inspection certificate, often called a beetle certificate, before a property is transferred. WDO work is a specialised registration category under Act 36 of 1947.

Termites

  • Subterranean termites live in colonies in the soil and reach timber through cracks in slabs, along foundations and inside earthen mud tubes. They hollow timber from inside, leaving a thin outer shell, and often fill galleries with soil. They are the most destructive termites of buildings in the warmer, wetter parts of the country.
  • Drywood termites live entirely inside dry timber, without soil contact. They produce small, hard, six-sided faecal pellets that fall from kick-out holes. They have been found in some coastal areas and are difficult to control without whole-structure treatment.
  • Harvester termites mainly damage veld and pasture rather than buildings.

Wood boring beetles

BeetleTimber attacked and signs
Common furniture beetleSoftwood and hardwood sapwood, furniture and floors; small round exit holes and gritty frass
Powderpost beetlesSapwood of certain hardwoods with high starch; very fine, flour-like frass
European house borerSoftwood such as pine roof timbers; larger oval exit holes and ripple-marked galleries. In the Western Cape it is subject to official control measures, so suspected cases must be reported as required.

Beetle larvae may feed inside timber for one to several years before adults emerge. Exit holes show past emergence; fresh frass and new holes indicate current activity.

Wood decay fungi

Fungi cause rot when timber stays damp, usually above about 20 percent moisture content. Brown rots make timber shrink, crack into cubes and crumble; white rots leave it pale, soft and stringy. Decay is a moisture problem first: without correcting leaks, rising damp or poor ventilation, any treatment will fail.

lessons.title: Inspection and assessment of timber pests
lessons.html:
Inspecting a property

A WDO inspection examines all accessible timber in and around a structure. Report clearly what was accessible and what was not, because concealed timber cannot be certified.

Where to look

  • Roof space: trusses, rafters, purlins, wall plates and ceiling brandering; look for exit holes, frass and galleries.
  • Interior: skirtings, door and window frames, floors, built-in cupboards and staircases.
  • Foundations and walls: mud tubes, cracks in slabs, expansion joints, plumbing penetrations.
  • Exterior: fascia boards, pergolas, decks, fences, wooden poles, firewood stacks and tree stumps near the building.
  • Wet areas: under sinks, around showers and roof leaks, where decay and termites are favoured.

Inspection techniques

  1. Visual inspection with a strong torch.
  2. Sounding: tap timber with a probe or screwdriver handle; hollow sounds suggest internal damage.
  3. Probing: test suspect timber for softness; avoid unnecessary damage to finishes.
  4. Moisture meter readings in timber near leaks or damp walls.
  5. Collect frass, pellets or specimens for identification.

Assessing activity and damage

Distinguish active infestation from old damage. Signs of activity include fresh, light-coloured frass, frass on top of dust, live insects, fresh mud tubes, and new exit holes. Estimate the extent of damage and whether structural members may be weakened. Where structural integrity is in doubt, recommend assessment by a structural engineer or builder.

The inspection report or certificate

  • Property, date, inspector and registration details.
  • Areas inspected and areas inaccessible.
  • Organisms found, their activity status and the timbers affected.
  • Conducive conditions, such as soil against timber, leaks and poor ventilation.
  • Recommendations for treatment, timber replacement and corrective building work.

Issue a clearance certificate only when you are satisfied that no active infestation is present in the accessible timbers, or after effective treatment. Never issue a certificate without a genuine inspection.

lessons.title: Treatment and prevention methods
lessons.html:
Choosing a treatment

The treatment depends on the organism, the extent of infestation, the structure and the situation. All chemical treatments must use products registered for the pest and use, applied as the label directs.

Subterranean termites

  • Pre-construction soil treatment: a registered termiticide is applied to the soil under slabs and along foundations before construction, creating a treated zone.
  • Post-construction treatment: trenching and treating soil along foundations, and drilling and injecting through slabs at cracks and penetrations.
  • Baiting systems: stations placed in the soil are monitored and baited with a slow-acting active ingredient that termites carry back to the colony.
  • Locate and treat or remove nests where accessible.

Take particular care to avoid contaminating wells, boreholes, drains, ponds and heating ducts.

Wood borers and drywood termites

  • Surface application of a registered timber insecticide to bare timber, by brush or spray, in roof spaces and on furniture.
  • Injection into exit holes or drilled holes for deeper penetration.
  • Fumigation of whole structures or furniture with a registered fumigant for severe or concealed infestations, by registered fumigators only.
  • Removal and replacement of severely damaged timber with treated timber.

Decay fungi

Find and fix the moisture source. Remove decayed timber beyond the affected area, improve ventilation and replace with treated timber. Treat adjacent timber with a registered preservative where appropriate.

Prevention

  • Use timber that has been preservative-treated to the correct hazard class for its use, and look for the treatment mark.
  • Keep soil, firewood and building rubble away from timber; maintain a gap between soil and woodwork.
  • Repair leaks and ensure roof spaces and sub-floors are ventilated.
  • Remove tree stumps and dead wood near buildings.
  • Inspect regularly.

Safety

Roof space work involves heat, dust, fragile ceilings, electrical wiring and confined working positions. Wear PPE, including a respirator where the label requires, stand only on structural members, and isolate power where wiring is damaged. Ventilate during and after treatment and keep occupants out for the time the label specifies.

Key points

  • WDOs include subterranean and drywood termites, wood boring beetles and decay fungi.
  • Fresh frass, live insects and new mud tubes indicate current activity; old holes may not.
  • Report inaccessible areas and never issue a certificate without a genuine inspection.
  • Match treatment to the organism: soil treatment or baiting for subterranean termites, timber treatment or fumigation for borers.
  • Decay is a moisture problem; fix the moisture source first.
